title: The Lantern of Vilna
premise: In 1938 Vilna, Vesper Dravenmoor, a quiet driver for the suffragist Miriam Kessler, secretly reads every letter he delivers and keeps a private archive of the city's voices in a lantern-lit workshop. When a census taker begins asking questions that suggest the state is cataloguing people for removal, Vesper realizes his invisible life of borrowed identities has made him the only one who can carry the neighborhood's stories to safety. As the orders come and the workshop is threatened, he must choose between erasing himself completely or becoming, at last, someone with a name worth remembering. The book ends with Vesper delivering the final letters after the workshop burns, planting the archive's seed pages abroad while staying behind as the keeper of what cannot be carried.
about_author: Astrid Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade restoring damaged letters from interwar Eastern Europe. She writes from a farmhouse in Jutland, where she keeps an unlit lantern on her desk in memory of the names she could not save.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Vesper Dravenmoor drives Miriam Kessler through Vilna's rain-slicked streets, delivering her suffragist correspondence while quietly reading each letter by lantern light in the workshop where he sleeps. His POV establishes his rule: know everything, belong to nothing. The emotional beat is the ache of intimacy without identity—he knows the whole city's secrets and no one knows his.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: A census taker named Brozek arrives at the Kessler house with unusually precise questions—not about households but about origins, names, and who sleeps where. Vesper, posing as 'the driver,' answers smoothly, but Brozek's notebook holds entries about the workshop. POV alternates to Brozek briefly, revealing a man who believes he is only doing arithmetic. The beat: dread arriving politely, in triplicate.

chapters.title: The Workshop of Small Fires
chapters.summary: Vesper returns to the lantern workshop run by old Tomas, where refugees copy documents and children learn letters by firelight—the found family Vesper never admits is his own. He confesses the census visit; Tomas dismisses it, but young Ruta copies the suspicious page numbers anyway. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: warmth sharpened by the first crack of fear running through it.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Miriam asks Vesper to deliver sealed packets to contacts in Kaunas, and he realizes she suspects more than she says—she tests him by including one letter addressed to a name Vesper used years ago. His POV, tense and watchful. The beat: the vertigo of being seen by the one person whose regard he wants, and the decision to finish the work rather than flee.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Names
chapters.summary: Brozek returns with corrections, and this time he asks Vesper directly: 'And your family name, driver?' Vesper gives a dead man's name and watches it written down, understanding that every false answer is now evidence. A second POV chapter from Brozek shows his doubt growing—he has begun noticing which names vanish from the ledgers. Beat: complicity and conscience circling each other.

chapters.title: Ruta's Lantern
chapters.summary: Ruta discovers Vesper's hidden archive of copied letters and confronts him: why keep everyone's words and claim none of your own? She demands to be taught the copying trade, forcing Vesper into the role of teacher—of family. His POV softens. Emotional beat: grief for the childhood he invented himself out of, transmuted into fierce protectiveness.

chapters.title: The Orders Come
chapters.summary: The first removal lists appear; neighbors disappear overnight, and Brozek's census pages are revealed as their source. Miriam's network mobilizes, and Vesper must drive through checkpoints carrying the archive's most dangerous pages sewn into his coat lining. His POV, breathless. Beat: the world measured now not in letters but in what fits against the ribs.

chapters.title: Brozek's Ledger
chapters.summary: Brozek, unable to unsee what his numbers have fed, comes to the workshop at night—not to arrest but to offer the missing pages that would let families alter their listings. Vesper must decide whether a collaborator's guilt can be trusted. Dual tension, Vesper's POV deciding. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of mercy—accepting help bought with others' erased names.

chapters.title: When the Workshop Stands No Longer
chapters.summary: Soldiers arrive to burn the workshop; Tomas refuses to leave and dies holding the door so Ruta and the copying plates escape through the cellar. Vesper carries the last lantern through smoke as the archive burns around them. Climax: Vesper screams his true name into the fire—the first time he has claimed it aloud. Beat: devastation fused with selfhood.

chapters.title: The Keeper of What Cannot Be Carried
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Vesper delivers the final letters—including one to Miriam confessing everything—and puts Ruta on the train to Kaunas with the seed pages, staying behind as the keeper of the neighborhood's memory. Miriam, having read his confession, calls him by his real name at last. Resolution: invisible no longer, he lights the salvaged lantern in a window. Beat: found family scattered but unbroken; memory as inheritance.
